title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
authors: Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.
summary: This paper explores the feasibility of enhancing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by integrating quantum layers, using classical simulations of quantum circuits. The research found that quantum integration can boost accuracy or reduce model size depending on where the layer is placed. It provides a detailed map of where quantum components might offer benefits, though the gains are not universally guaranteed.
main_problem: The study investigates whether integrating quantum layers into Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can yield performance or security advantages over purely classical architectures.
main_result: Quantum insertion can improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce trainable parameters, but these benefits are highly dependent on the layer's specific location within the VLM.
method: The authors used classically simulated quantum circuits (4- and 8-qubit) to test both inserting and replacing classical components within a VLM backbone, while also evaluating adversarial robustness.
model_or_system: The system is a Vision-Language Model (VLM), specifically using LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, augmented with quantum-classical hybrid layers.
key_observables: Predictive accuracy (e.g., 80.7% on Visual Spatial Reasoning), reduction in trainable parameters (e.g., 13.07 million fewer), and adversarial robustness under six attack settings.
important_parameters: Qubit count (4- and 8-qubits), circuit type (basic-ring, strongly entangling), and insertion/replacement locations within the VLM structure.
main_assumptions: The study relies on classical simulation of quantum layers, and the observed gains may not generalize to actual quantum hardware or different model architectures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the proposed framework showing quantum layer insertion and replacement locations in the VLM backbone, and detail the specific quantum circuits used (BR4, BR8, SE4, SE8).
paper_structure: The paper systematically tests quantum layer integration via insertion and replacement across multiple VLM components, comparing performance, computational cost, and robustness against various adversarial attacks.
why_interesting: While the focus is on AI, the methodology involves mapping quantum circuit structures (basic-ring, strongly entangling) onto deep learning architectures, which touches upon the concept of quantum information processing within complex computational models.
